What progress has been made over the past year by scientists working under the direction of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys in matters related to the bituminous sands of northeastern Alberta, with particular reference to economic mining of the sands, separation of bitumen from the sand, and processing of bitumen into usable products, and any other progress towards utilization of the bituminous sands?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
The question asked relates to the work during the past year of the scientists of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys on the problems of utilizing the bituminous sands of Alberta. In this period the scientists have designed, installed and operated a small low-pressure hydrogenation plant and in their experiments have successfully removed the high sulphur content from gas oil derived from bitumen. The gas oil is a field product that would be distilled from bitumen derived by either the cold-water or hot-water method of separating the bitumen from the sands

and it is necessary to design a further step or process in which sulphur is removed before the oil, which would otherwise be very corrosive and unacceptable, is pipelined to refineries. The application of hydrogenation provides one of the important fundamental answers required by industry and Mr. S. M. Blair, the technical consultant employed by the Alberta government. This work on hydrogenation is being pursued intensively to obtain proper data for its commercial application and when put into practice there would be important by-product recovery of sulphur, a mineral in very short supply.
During the year the mines branch of the department has also proceeded intensively with the obtaining of equipment and its installation in a laboratory designed for extensive fundamental research in hydrogenation at variable pressures up to an extreme high pressure of 20,000 pounds per square inch. This plant will work on the Alberta bitumen problem and it may be that the eventual most economic utilization of the tar sands for production of gasoline and other high-grade fuels will involve a wider use of the hydrogenation process than its mere application to sulphur removal.
One of the laboratories has also been engaged in fundamental studies of the constitution of bitumen and throughout the year the federal scientists have been in close consultation .and collaboration with the technical consultant of the Alberta government. At the symposium on the bituminous sands held in Edmonton last September, which was largely attended by representatives of the oil industry, the department was represented by its director general of scientific services, Dr. George S. Hume, who is a leading oil geologist and by a group of scientists from the federal mines branch. These scientists took a leading part in the conference by their presentation of papers on the work the dominion government has carried out to assist exploitation of the bituminous or oil sand resources of Alberta.
It is necessary to a proper understanding of the present work to have some background information. Following many years of work by mines branch on surface exploration of the deposits and on preliminary studies of uses for the bitumen, the dominion government in 1942 embarked on a project to definitely find workable deposits for their oil content and to determine the practicability of producing gasoline and high-grade fuels. This program on the one hand consisted of extensive drilling. A method had to be found which would properly sample the deposits at depth and when successful

Questions
core-drilling had been accomplished the method was applied over extensive areas. This work during 1942 to 1947 produced the first information on which actual exploitation of the deposits could be based. Its most important finding was the location in the vicinity of the Mildred-Ruth lakes, 20 miles north of Fort McMurrav, of a deposit of better grade sands containing, in an area of four and a half square miles, 900 million barrels of oil or sufficient to operate a twenty thousand barrel per day oil plant for more than one hundred years.
Concurrently with starting the drilling for workable deposits the federal scientists and engineers joined efforts on the economic aspects of exploiting the oil sands with Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada Limited and Abasand Oils Limited, the latter the only organization with a plant for separation operations.
Oil froth separated from the sands was shipped to Universal Oil Products Company in Chicago and pilot plant tests there gave the first definite information on the possibilities of the bituminous sands for producing standard commercial petroleum products. It was still necessary to develop an efficient method for separating the very heavy oil from the sands and a field process to remove its heavy characteristics and sulphur.
The Abasand Oils Limited plant was rebuilt with federal aid and tests were made of the McClave hot-water process. Before the plant was destroyed accidentally by fire in 1945 a start had been made at developing a cold-water process which was later fully developed by test runs in a pilot plant installed at the mines branch in Ottawa, which plant was also used to develop means for reducing the heavy oil to a light gas oil.
Thus the scientists of the department have been engaged in a consecutive, co-ordinated investigation designed to assist the oil industry and the Alberta government in determining the best and most practicable means of utilizing the oil in the bituminous sands and through the current work is providing an answer to the problem of how to remove sulphur from the intermediate gas-oil product.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO REPORTS TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was wondering what gave rise to this particular bill. One can easily see the object of it, but have there been any cases where the effect of the law as it stands at present would have required the tabling of any report at two sessions of parliament in the same year?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO REPORTS TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Yes. If my hon. friend will examine, for example, the Department of Insurance Act, 1932, chapter 45, section 9, he will find that it reads as follows:
The minister shall lay before parliament within thirty days after the commencement of each session thereof the annual report of the superintendent made to the minister under the provisions of each of the acts specified in the schedule to this act.
A literal interpretation of that section would require, I think, an annual filing of the report in question and of all subsequent reports.
Another example is in the Penitentiary Act, 1939, chapter 6, section 14, which provides:
The minister shall submit to the governor in council an annual report upon the penitentiaries, prisons and other institutions under his control, to be laid before both houses of parliament within the first twenty-one days of each session thereof . . .
These are just drafting errors which it is the purpose of this present bill to cure in all cases in which they have occurred. This bill will require the tabling, as I think was the intention of parliament, of each of these reports in one session, namely the session which takes place next after their preparation.

APPROVAL OF SUPPLEMENTARY CONVENTION BETWEEN UNITED STATES AND CANADA SIGNED ON OCTOBER 26, 1951 Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the supplementary extradition convention between the United States of America and Canada, signed at Ottawa on October 26, 1951, amending the supplementary extradition convention between the United States of America and Her Britannic Majesty, signed at Washington on December 13, 1900, and that this house do approve the same.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make several brief comments on this extradition treaty. I have no doubt that it will receive general (Mr. Fleming.]

support in the house. Nevertheless I think there are two or three observations which may perhaps usefully be made.
Those who sat in the house in 1945 will not soon forget the extradition convention of that time which was submitted to this house for ratification and was then referred by the house to the standing committee on external affairs for study and review. In the committee that extradition convention was found to be one unworthy of the support of the house. The committee held extensive hearings during the course of which they heard many representations, all of them adverse to the convention.
The distinguishing feature of that particular extradition convention was a long list of extraditable offences which were created, which had no counterpart in the criminal law of Canada, and which would in effect have created, for the purpose of extradition to the United States, offences which were then not offences under the criminal law of Canada.
I think it is worth observing, sir, that the standing committee on external affairs at that time rendered an important public service in providing an opportunity for many persons and organizations interested in the subject to make their representations to a public body or organ of this House of Commons; and in arriving at the conclusion that the committee could not recommend the ratification of that convention I consider the committee also rendered an important and useful service.
Now, sir, the convention before the house at the present time is a very different-looking document from that of 1945. To that extent it is a substantial improvement. Actually it purports to introduce two amendments only in section 11 of the extradition convention between Canada and the United States of December 13, 1900. These two amendments, sir, do have counterparts in the criminal law of this country. We were assured in the committee that the proposed new section 11A of the convention has its counterpart in sections 404	and 444	of	the	Criminal
Code, and the proposed new section 11B has its counterpart in section 209 of the Criminal Code.
Sir, there has been a good deal of publicity given to negotiations leading up to this convention; and	it may	not	be	amiss topoint out the limitations on the scope of this convention. Considerable publicity has been given to the operation of certain Canadian stock salesmen who use the mails or the telegraph or the	telephone	in	the	course oftheir efforts to sell stocks	to	United States
buyers, and whose communications, in the course of those efforts, pass the international boundary.
I think there are some sections of the public who have come to the conclusion that this extradition [DOT] convention will have the effect of making it an extraditable offence to convey certain forms of representations in connection with the sale of stock by Canadian salesmen speaking in Canada over the telephone to persons in the United States, or sending telegrams from Canadian points to persons resident in the United States. At its meeting on May 13, the committee on external affairs had an opportunity of clarifying the effect of this convention. And may I again point out, sir, that as in 1945, and as on a good many other occasions, the standing committee on external affairs has rendered an important and useful service in connection with this convention.
The matter was clarified to this extent that when Mr. Varcoe, the deputy minister of justice, was asked questions with reference to the limitations of the convention, the matter was summed up finally in this question and answer at page 283 of the proceedings of the committee on external affairs on May 13. I asked this question:
It is quite clear that representations made across the border by someone in Canada by telephone, telegraph, radio or television would not be within the scope of this treaty and would not be an extraditable offence?

I would think it would not.
And, sir, that answer, as well as answers given to other questions in the course of the hearing in the committee, make it quite clear that the only form in which misrepresentations become the occasion of the commission of an extraditable offence is when those communications are committed to the post office, and when the United States mails, in the course of transportation of those written communications, are used in the course of forwarding or delivery.
There is one other matter, sir, that did interest the committee, and it does interest a number of Canadian dealers in securities, who are carrying on a quite legitimate and proper business. I am sure hon. members are aware of the difficulties that have confronted a great many issues, oftentimes small issues, of Canadian securities at the hands of the securities exchange commission of the United States, whose standards are exceedingly rigid, and were written with regard to the fact that in the United States the securities business relates more-at least to a greater extent than in Canada-to the securities of established enterprises, and much less than in Canada to the securities of corporations and syndicates issued in the course of
Supplementary Extradition Convention pioneer development work, or as we speak of it, enterprises involving the use of risk capital.
There has been under discussion for some time a proposal on the part of the securities exchange commission of the United States for easing its requirements with reference to small issues of stock which Canadian corporations may desire to market in the United States. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), when appearing before the committee, very properly drew attention to this fact, and to the prospect held out of some alleviation for smaller Canadian stock issues proposed to be marketed in the United States of the very rigid requirements now imposed on all such issues by the securities exchange commission.
At page 286 of the proceedings the minister had this to say:

Mr. Chairman, I do not want
unduly to influence the decision of the committee at this stage, but I think that I should point out that the brokers who are in business of raising this money in Canada were rather interested in getting a short term of registration in the United States, and the chairman of the American Securities Commission giving evidence in the United States the other day concerning this supplementary extradition convention with Canada said:
"I think the committee should be aware of the fact that the commission is giving consideration to providing some kind of short form registration for small Canadian offerings, and upon ratification of this treaty by both nations would probably proceed to do something along those lines."
I think it would be very much in the interests of the investment industry here that this should be approved as soon as we can, and then they could proceed to get this short-form of registration which is so much desired by the investment fraternity in Canada.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that observation was very properly put before the committee by the Minister of Justice, and in further questions and answers the minister did give assurance to the committee that the government would make representations in this behalf in order that this desirable easing of the strict requirements of the securities exchange commission should be brought about in so far as the marketing of small issues of Canadian stocks and securities in the United States is concerned.
Sir, there is one final matter I should like to mention. It does not arise directly out of the terms of the convention; nevertheless I think it is a proper matter for comment in the discussion of this measure at the present stage.
There are some who, when hearing of sales of Canadian stocks to Americans, under conditions of high pressure, leap to the conclusion that there are many Canadians engaged in this nefarious form of the sale of securities, and who seek to put all, or at
2426	HOUSE OF
Supplementary Extradition Convention least many, Canadians who are engaged in the securities business in the same category.
I wish to enter an emphatic protest against conclusions of that kind because, as you well know, Mr. Speaker, they are not warranted. Those engaged in Canada in the securities business are, in the overwhelming majority, people who are honest, and who are carrying on a perfectly legitimate and useful trade. Simply that there happen to be a few renegades, or high-pressure artists, is no reason whatever for heaping opprobrium and suspicion upon the great majority of those who are properly engaged in this very legitimate and necessary business.
And, sir, there is one aspect of the subject in which in the past the actions taken by certain American governmental officers have been highly improper. It is not unusual for Canadians in recent times to receive from officials of the American government or state governments, subpoenas delivered in Canada, if you please, to appear before commissions or officials in the United States, and to bring with them the books and records of Canadian corporations. Situations of that kind have been brought to the attention of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson).
I know he has intervened in such cases, pointing out to the American authorities that their writ does not run in Canada, and that when officers of any American government, whether federal or state, undertake to issue orders to Canadians in Canada either to appear personally before American boards or commissions or to produce books and records in that country, they have no right to do so.
Think of the position in which Canadians have been placed by the issuance of such unauthorized orders and subpoenas, when they are served in Canada without any authority or warrant. When Canadians have chosen to ignore these unauthorized subpoenas and orders, as they are quite entitled to do, it has meant that if at any time in the future they enter the United States they have thereby rendered themselves subject to detention.
That has been a high-handed action on the part of many American governmental officers against which I think it is quite proper in this place to protest very strongly.
It is not to be supposed that these subpoenas and orders have been issued simply in the case of Canadian salesmen who have been attempting to sell their securities by high-pressure methods. Far from it. In many cases these have been served upon Canadians only by registered mail, Canadians who are carrying on a perfectly legitimate business here in Canada, and without any offence under the laws of either Canada or the United States.


I hope Canadians will not be subjected to high-handed and unauthorized interference of this kind. It should be made clear to all American governmental authorities that the American writ does not run in Canada. The only writ that runs in Canada is the writ of Canada or of any province.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a witness who appeared before the committee on external affairs, I should like to deal with some points of law connected with this resolution, and to express my appreciation of the attitude shown by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, not only in the speech he has just delivered in this chamber but in the constructive analysis he made of the resolution when it was before the external affairs committee.
With the greater part of what he has said today, and what he said then, I find myself in agreement. I think it should be rather difficult to imagine any argument more convincing for the support of this resolution than the one he has just made. There are however one or two points he raised about which I should like to make a few observations, in order to complete the picture for those members who are not lawyers.
He has said that on previous occasions the effort of the United States government has been to secure an extradition treaty covering these matters, in which the principle of single criminality would be observed. That is to say, the United States government previously wished to extradite Canadian citizens from Canada to the United States to stand trial there for an offence which was a crime under American law but not under Canadian law.
Thanks to the stand taken by my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), that position of the American government was resisted, with the result that we have here an extradition treaty in which the principle of double criminality has been strictly observed. Under this treaty no Canadian can be taken from Canada under an extradition order until application has been made under the treaty to a Canadian court, and until lawyers representing the United States government can convince that Canadian court that there is evidence establishing a prima facie case against such Canadian under the law in Canada which is analogous to the American law for an alleged breach of which the Canadian citizen would be tried if extradited to the United States. In that way a Canadian citizen has ample protection against being extradited, unless and until a Canadian court has first been satisfied that a prima facie case has been made out against him here.

When the Canadian citizen is extradited to the United States he can there be charged under the American analogue of the law in Canada under which the extradition application in the Canadian court was made. If he is found guilty, of course he has to bear punishment. If on the other hand he is acquitted there he must be released and cannot be charged in the United States for the breach of any other law of that country.
It can be seen from this that no legitimate businessman, who has not been guilty of an offence against the laws either of Canada or of the United States, stands in any appreciable jeopardy of being extradited under this treaty. Indeed the interests of all the legitimate investment dealers have been greatly served by the conclusion of this treaty because, as the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) said, one of the things which the legitimate businessmen in Canada have long desired in order to get American risk capital for investment in this country has been some method whereby it would be possible to put Canadian stock issues upon the market in the United States without going through the very expensive and cumbersome regulations of the securities exchange commission of that country.
The rule in that country is that the securities exchange commission have the discretionary power to exempt issues not exceeding $300,000 in any one year of United States companies provided that they complete the short form application only. That is a much more simple and economical method than having to comply with the very stringent regulations of the securities exchange commission. The position which the United States authorities have taken consistently up until the present time is that they are not desirous of extending the privilege of selling stock issues in that country under the short-form registration unless they are satisfied that they have available in their law in connection with the sale of such issues sanctions against fraud or other such forms of irregularity. As they put it, the existence of these broad sanctions is the premise upon which the grants of exemption from full compliance with their long-form regulations by the securities exchange commission is based. The securities exchange commission has taken the position in the United States in relation to domestic stock issues, and it takes the same position with regard to foreign stock issues, that under the law they could not properly extend exemptions to any situation where these sanctions against fraud did not exist. They obviously do not exist in the case of an offerer of stock residing in a country with which the United States
Supplementary Extradition Convention does not have an extradition treaty with a reasonable fraud coverage. The United States contention has been that the fraud coverage which prevailed formerly under the treaty of 1900 was not sufficiently wide to cover them in the case of short-form issues.
It follows from that by a process of logic, which they have not attempted to deny or resist, that if such treaty should be agreed upon, and especially if the requisite sanctions against fraud could be made possible, the commission would give sympathetic consideration to such a request for a short-form registration, and would endeavour to work out for legitimate business in Canada a method by which they could have recourse to this short-form registration in the United States. This is a privilege which I think I am safe in saying is considered of great value by Canadian promoters and investment dealers.
The quotation which the hon. member for Eglinton referred to in his remarks of a few minutes ago as having been used by myself before our external affairs committee was from a statement by commissioner R. B. McEntire, of the securities exchange commission in the United States. He made the following statement in March of this year before the committee on foreign relations of the United States Senate:
I think the committee should be aware of the fact that the commission is giving consideration to providing some kind of short-form registration for small Canadian offerings, and upon ratification of this treaty by both nations would probably proceed to do something along those lines.
It seems to me that this is going as far as any civil servant could go under the circumstances under which this statement was made. For these reasons, especially the ones which the hon. member for Eglinton has so eloquently put forward, I think it is distinctly in the interests of the legitimate businessmen of Canada and of Canada itself- it is against only the interests of fraudulent promoters and stock salesmen-that we should pass this resolution as soon as possible and thereby endeavour to secure this short-form registration privilege to which we attach considerable value.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say just a few words on this resolution. A rather extraordinary thing happened in the 1945 committee. The report throwing out the treaty was not introduced by the government, it was spoken to by myself. The objections to that treaty were four in number and I think it would be of interest to state at this time what those objections were and why that previous treaty was so unacceptable. I should like to quote from

Supplementary Extradition Convention my remarks as they appear on page 3711 of Hansard of December 17, 1945, as follows:
Basically the principles which the treaty violated were these. First, it did away with the time-honoured and, I believe, historic principle of dual criminality.
And again:
The second fundamental point which the committee felt was detrimental to the acceptance of this instrument was that the treaty by its various clauses greatly enlarged the offences for which extradition might be sought . . .
And again:
The third reason-and this was an important one -was that we were not satisfied that the treaty and protocol as drawn were not ultra vires of this parliament with regard to the rights of property and civil rights as vested in the provinces under the British North America Act.
Finally:
Then-and this is not a legal point; it is perhaps a physical point-we felt that the restrictive clauses which were mentioned in the treaty, subsections 26, 31, 32, article III, article IX and article XII, section 1 of the treaty, would definitely restrict the opening up of our great natural resources.
I went on to state the reasons why the treaty was thrown out. That treaty completely abrogated many of the sovereign rights of Canada. It was just about as bad a treaty as could be imagined. I think this instrument is acceptable because it overcomes these four cardinal sins, if I can so term them. As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) has said, it opens up the possibility of short-form registration privileges being granted to Canadians.
I submit that that is most important. A normal prospectus under the S.E.C. may run anywhere from fifty to one hundred pages of small type and be so involved and so labyrinthine in character as to defy most lawyers getting to the bottom of its meaning. As a matter of fact, I have heard it said that they are made as complicated, as long and as involved as possible so that the actual facts can be submerged at times in a tidal wave of verbiage. They defeat their own ends.
I see no objection to this treaty. From what the minister has said, I think it will be of assistance to the legitimate Canadian businessman. First of all, a prima facie case must be made out that the law of Canada has been contravened and broken. Second, and this also is of great importance, if extradition is granted the person so extradited cannot be charged for any other offence. As a matter of fact that was one of the great dangers of the first instrument in that, if extradition was asked for, one state after another could then bring subsequent charges for other offences which might entail the ruination of the person so extradited or his incarceration for almost the rest of his natural

life. Having said that, I believe that this is a step that should be taken. I think it will assist development in many ways. Many of our development companies start off in a very small way. There are chances of a small investment, particularly in the mining and oil fields, leading to very great profits, but that type of investment is of necessity hazardous and extremely speculative. Nevertheless it is an essential part of the economy of Canada, and to restrict it in any way would in my opinion seriously jeopardize the continued prosperity of our industry.
Motion agreed to.

I should like to deal very briefly with one or two of the points that have been raised. Of course, it is our understanding that there should be a fairly wide discussion of this whole question in the standing committee. I do not believe there will be any effort on anyone's part to restrict the discussion to the terms of this particular bill, because when we discussed these matters in the standing committee before, it was understood that there would be an occasion for a further examination of the treaty of peace, even though the treaty had already been ratified. At that time there was need for speedy action in order to bring the treaty into effect, and that was appreciated by the members of the committee. It was also understood by them that there would be an opportunity for further discussion. If it is submitted to the committee, this bill will provide that opportunity.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked me if I could indicate generally the kind of regulation which might be issued under this enabling legislation. He mentioned the question of penalties. We will have at the committee meetings, Mr. Speaker, legal, economic and other experts who will be able to go into this in considerable detail. Provision for penalties

Treaty of Peace (Japan) Act has been embodied in the legislation in case penalties may be required. But up to the present, for instance under the analogous legislation implementing the treaties of peace with Italy and certain other countries which was passed a couple of years ago, it has been found necessary to issue only two orders in council and no penalties have been required in the light of those orders in council. However, as this bill is designed to make effective upon Canadian nationals certain obligations contracted by the government of Canada and approved in due course, I hope, by the parliament of Canada, it is usual in such cases to provide for a penalty clause against emergencies.
As to the type of regulation which may be required, I might give two examples which would indicate to the hon. member what may be necessary under the treaty of peace with Japan. Article 14(a) of the peace treaty, for instance, exempts certain property from the general provision mentioned in an earlier part of the treaty, that all Japanese property should be turned over to the Canadian government and could be utilized for the payment of compensation. Exempted from that clause is certain diplomatic property. Regulations may be required to make that exemption effective in our domestic legislation. This bill to implement the peace treaty may, in effect, bind Canadians, and for that purpose certain orders in council may be required.
To take another example this time from the treaty of peace with Italy, a lump sum settlement was negotiated to clear up all our claims against Italy and all Italian claims against us. Order in council P.C. 5818 of November 6, 1951, was issued under the Treaties of Peace (Italy, Roumania, Hungary and Finland) Act of 1948 and it was known as the "war claims (Italy) settlement regulations". It contained a provision by which the payment to Canada by Italy of the agreed lump sum constituted satisfaction by Italy of its obligations to Canada and to Canadian nationals. The effect of this provision would be to prevent a Canadian from suing in a Canadian court to recover a war claim. A similar kind of regulation may, in the future, be required under this proposed legislation if it becomes effective. That is the type of thing that may be done under an order in council, and when this matter is discussed before the standing committee on external affairs, other detailed examples can be given by the experts who will be present.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION SIGNED BY CANADA ON NOVEMBER 28, 1949
speechtext:
should like to say a few words about this resolution. It is much too important to let pass without some comment. Here is an attempt to have the conscience of the world express itself through law. We should remember that it is only an attempt, and nothing more. There are no teeth in this legislation by which we could make it operative, but at least it is a start to something better. There are those who profess to scorn attempts such as this which they say are merely gestures. But a gesture perhaps has its importance in the world today. Furthermore what is looked upon as merely illegal can eventually become immoral.
I remember reading in history of the situation which prevailed in the United Kingdom over a hundred years ago when it was regarded as right and proper that women and children should work for ten and twelve hours a day in the coal mines. Some people were horrified at what was happening. Eventually legislation was passed prohibiting this practice. It was then illegal, and has now become immoral as well as illegal. In time I hope that the intent of this resolution

will be accepted throughout the whole world, and be just as illegal as it is immoral. There can be no question at all that the people of this country support the resolution. This I would say is especially true of one particular group, organized labour, for genocide has not been practised only against people of certain religious views or certain ethnic groups. It has been practiced against social groups, and modern history relates that the working class groups in Europe have suffered under this form of mass murder.
The ratification of the resolution will mean that the crime of genocide is always before us. That is a good thing, for our memories are short. I wonder how many of even my generation remember the crimes which were perpetrated at the beginning of the century against the Armenians. Most of us have forgotten them. I wonder how many remember the crimes which were perpetrated against the Ukrainian people in soviet Russia in the early thirties when, through deliberate policy of the men in the Kremlin, millions of Ukrainians were exterminated in what the Russians conceived to be their national interest. I have heard the number put as low as 6 million and I have heard it placed as high as 15 million; but I think at least 8 million Ukrainians were exterminated in the early part of the thirties. That was a crime which was not perhaps internationally illegal then but which we now hope to make illegal.
We remember, after the war, when tens of thousands of Poles and Lithuanians were exterminated, again as acts of policy on the part of the Russians. We remember what happened to the Sudeten Germans as a group. I think the world particularly remembers the horrors which happened to the Jewish people under nazi Germany when some 6 or 7 million of them were exterminated, again in the name of national policy.
The question, however, is whether the next generation will remember these horrible things. Many of them will forget; but I am certain that in my constituency they will remember, for 50 per cent of the people whom I represent have been affected or afflicted in one way or another by this wretched crime of genocide. Not only does genocide destroy bodies but, what is just as bad, it can destroy minds. If it can destroy minds, it can destroy cultures; and wherever a culture is lost to the world, to that extent all of us are impoverished.
Even though this legislation be nothing more than a pious aspiration just now, nevertheless in the long run, as it becomes accepted, we can hope that it will raise general standards throughout the world; for today- and this applies not only to those who are
Genocide Convention
behind the iron curtain-there are groups so harassed that they can think only of survival. They have time to think of nothing else. If we can make this resolution become operative throughout the world, these groups will be given some security so they can devote their energies to building up a better life.
We are glad to have before us this resolution to ratify the convention. We are glad to see it ratified, but ratification by 32 nations, Mr. Speaker, is not enough. It must be ratified by all countries in the world and I should like to see it done-although at the moment it is impossible-without any reservation whatsoever. Meanwhile those who refuse to ratify this convention must stand condemned by the world.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this resolution is one that received considerable attention in the external affairs committee a few days ago. One of the members of the official opposition, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), has given a great deal of close and sympathetic attention and study to this convention on the prevention and punishment of the crime of genocide.
