subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION SIGNED BY CANADA ON NOVEMBER 28, 1949
speechtext:
Perhaps some may think the business was made more urgent by the fact that the minister himself has not been here for the last couple of days. I hope neither one of them has been engaged in anything that indicates a question of political genocide. In any event, I wanted to indicate to the minister why I am taking the part I am taking in connection with this debate today.
I have followed closely the discussions in the external affairs committee, and I think everyone has been of the opinion that Canada, in becoming a signatory to the convention on genocide, found herself in the position of agreeing to something which was, in a sense, half a loaf rather than a whole one. I think we all realize that even though we ratify the convention on genocide, it goes only part way in executing what Canadians generally would like to see accomplished and achieved in this matter.
I suppose there is no other country in the world whose people are more quickly outraged by news of this kind of mass extermination of groups. It is so foreign to the Canadian way of thinking that perhaps we are apt sometimes to look at it from afar. But there are in Canada many people whose relatives have suffered under this kind of persecution. Even though the convention does not go

Genocide Convention
nearly as far as Canadians would like to see it go, so far as its effect is concerned, I think it would have been a great mistake if Canada had not taken her stand. I think that we in Canada were wise, both at the United Nations and also here in the external affairs committee, to take our stand against this kind of international outlawry and try to do our part as best we can to establish some measure of law, order and simple justice for people the world over.
That is one of the reasons we support this convention. It is not as effective as it might be. As members of the house and of the external affairs committee will agree, it has grave limitations. Nevertheless it at least provides a moral if not a legal sanction with respect to this type of injustice wherever it occurs. I should like, however, to point out that with respect to the ratification of this convention, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) a moment ago, only some 32 out of the 60 members of the United Nations have endorsed it so far as their parliaments are concerned, or have signed the convention itself.
Strangely enough, the three so-called leading powers in the world have not so far become actual ratifying parties to the convention. The United States congress has not yet come to any conclusion with respect to this convention. There have been debates there of a rather extensive nature in connection with it, but so far the ratification has not been completed. In addition to that, the United Kingdom has not only not ratified the convention, but has not become a signatory to it. Then there is the further fact that the soviet Union-as one perhaps might now be led to expect in matters of this kind-in ratifying and signing the convention put in so many joker clauses by way of exempting their country from its operation that it is not of great importance so far as that nation is concerned today. It seems to me that behind the iron curtain is perhaps the very place where we need this law applied, and the iron curtain countries evidently have taken the position that they are going to have so many reservations in the convention that it will not matter a great deal to them whether it is law or not. That is not a very satisfactory arrangement from Canada's point of view. It is a disappointing situation because surely we have gone far enough in our thinking and in our actions that all the nations of the world ought to be able at least to come to one conclusion, namely that it is wrong and unjust for this kind of international crime to go unpunished, as it apparently has in the past.
[Mr. Graydon.l
It sometimes makes one despair of world opinion when he realizes that we seem to be able to go only such a short way in trying to rid the world of such a menace as this. However, in the committee on external affairs the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) entered into a discussion with other hon. members and with the parliamentary assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. At that time I understood a point had been reached in connection with that part of the convention which, in defining what genocide means in subsection (b) of article II, mentions causing bodily or mental harm to members of a group, where some question arose with respect to the words "mental harm." I understood that was a matter which had engaged the attention not only of the United States congress but of some other nations as well, because of the varying degrees of interpretation which have been placed upon these words.
Perhaps there is no great reason why we should not ratify it even with those words in it, but I would ask the minister, when he closes this debate, to take into consideration such undertaking as the parliamentary assistant gave in the committee so it will be made clear to parliament and to the world just what the Canadian parliament means when it endorses the convention with these two words included in it.
I have no very strong feelings myself with regard to the inclusion of those words. In my mind it is only a question of how we can make the most effective and workable convention and have it ratified by this parliament, so it will go forward to the world as a message that after all the Canadian people are taking this means, perhaps a feeble one, but nevertheless the only means that seems to be at hand at the moment, to tell the world that this country is shocked, startled and concerned over crimes of this kind which have been perpetrated in the past, and that it is not going to stand for any repetition in the days that lie ahead.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION SIGNED BY CANADA ON NOVEMBER 28, 1949
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am particularly glad of the opportunity which is presented here for me to discuss the genocide convention, which I consider of great importance. I feel sure the house will unanimously endorse the convention. The world now and then requires reminders of acts which it would rather forget. The memory of man being what it is, it is necessary from time to time to repeat some vital matters that perhaps would better be left unsaid.
This convention on genocide strikes at the very root of the problem which is facing the world today. It is a problem bound up not only with the interests of persons but

with the interests of groups throughout the length and breadth of the world, those who hold different religious views and different political points of view. It is particularly bound up with the possibility of peace throughout the world.
The United Nations, which exists for the specific purpose of trying to get the nations of the world to iron out their difficulties is, in my opinion, one of the most effective methods of eventually destroying the possibility of war. The general assembly of the United Nations on December 9, 1948, adopted a convention to outlaw genocide. That convention was accepted unanimously.
Genocide is mass murder. It is a modern name for an old crime. It means the destruction of whole groups of people just because they belong to particular groups. The group may be radical or national, or it may be religious. It may be a particular ethnical or racial group. The destruction may take various forms. Genocide has destroyed some 20 million persons in the last fifty years. I quote these figures with great humility. In the first half of the twentieth century alone the crime of genocide was perpetrated against the following human groups: Armenians, 10,000 at the turn of the century; Jews, several hundred thousand in 1902 and 1905 in Russia and in other European countries; Armenians, 1,200,000 in 1915 and 1916; Greeks, about 500,000 in Smyrna in 1922; Ukrainians, millions of them since the occupation of their territory by the Soviet; Jews, under the nazis, 6 million; Serbs, 800,000 in the so-called independent state of Croatia; Poles, 3 million since 1939: Lithuanians, 600,000 since 1941 and still continuing; Latvians, 400,000 since 1941 and still continuing; Estonians, between a quarter and a third of the entire population since 1941 and still continuing.
I am not going to read the rest. You have a fair idea of what the record indicates has happened almost within our own lifetime. In modern days the nazis developed their technique which was use particularly against racial and religious groups, til-Jews, and against the national linguistic group, the Poles.
The crime of genocide is not new; it has been practised under different names since the destruction of Carthage by the Romans. Throughout the middle ages there were the Jewish pogroms, the mass killings in various countries of Europe. In the last century, the mass killings of Armenians and again in this century the persecution of the Armenians in the Ottoman empire were horrible examples.
Genocide Convention
Individuals, groups, yes, nations, and Canada amongst them, were often aroused to protest against these massacres, but nothing more was done about it. It was the systematic brutalities practised by the nazis that shocked the conscience of the twentieth century. The twentieth century conscience refused to accept the dictum that the horrible atrocities they committed on these people were matters within domestic jurisdiction. So the world decided to concern itself. It was recognized at Nuremberg that there were crimes against humanity, that these crimes must be punished by law, and they were so punished. It is true that at Nuremberg those charged and convicted were tried on a basis of retroactive law. There was no law in existence which specifically covered these crimes. I believe the world is still firmly of the opinion that no injustice was done at that time.
It became clear that international law would have to be developed to deal with the international crime of genocide. There are already examples of laws for dealing with certain international crimes: Slave trade, illegal production and trade in narcotics, piracy, trade in women and children. International conventions have been signed on these crimes, and anyone guilty of them can be tried and punished not only in his own country but in whatever country he escapes to, provided that country has adhered to the convention. This convention is merely extending an international convention to genocide.
We in this country have a long and distinguished record for being in the forefront of humanitarian efforts. Canada was one of those countries that officially protested against the treatment of the Jews and others by the nazis. Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, as he was then known, was the prime minister who boldly and courageously spoke for Canada in words that rang throughout the world as a clarion call for freedom and justice when he protested against the treatment the nazis were dealing out to these people. It follows that the prevention of genocide is in line with the overwhelming opinion and feeling of the people of Canada. It has great and deep appeal to many of our minority groups.
I speak with some knowledge. I have seen some of the things with which this convention deals. I have seen the victims of these happenings. I have met and known men and women whose whole families have been sent to the gas chambers and who have seen them tortured and afflicted. I have seen the gas chambers. That kind of thing we cannot tolerate.
I recall the first time I saw a gas chamber. I wondered what it was, but I soon found out, Today, years later, I still shudder as

Genocide Convention
I recall vividly those gas chambers. It was a horrifying experience long remembered which burns and sears the memory. It was in the early days of 1945, when we were moving across Europe rather quickly, with the Germans in retreat. I remember the first camp in which there was a gas chamber. I recall particularly the meticulous records the nazis kept. Nothing was left to chance. Nothing was hidden. The records were perfect. On one side of the ledger the heading was Juden; on the other side were inscribed other unfortunate persons of all nationalities. The side of the ledger headed Juden was by far the largest. But there were far too many on the other side, also.
So I am particularly happy today to know that this House of Commons will make a decision, which I have already indicated in my opinion will be unanimous, to endorse this convention, which is in keeping with our position as one of the leaders of the middle nations. We are giving leadership, as the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) has pointed out, both to the United States and the United Kingdom, neither of which has yet ratified the convention, though neither is ever likely to be charged with the offence of genocide. Sometimes even that is doubtful, in view of the germ charges made by the communists and their stooges, which are false, dishonest and even worse than that. But it indicates that these matters have an importance beyond their immediate perspective.
This genocide convention is a step against jungle law. It is a recognition of the wrongs which have been inflicted on helpless people. It is a proclamation that the rights of man do not belong to the strong alone, or to the privileged few. For that reason this document or any other document cannot compensate for the loss suffered, not merely by the innocent victims but by the world.
We are all responsible in some measure for the terrible persecutions of our time, which I indicated to the house a few moments ago. Those of us who stand by and permit these crimes to be committed cannot escape some portion of the guilt. So this genocide convention today is an admission and a recognition by us of our responsibility, and our solemn pledge that the sins of the past will not be allowed to repeat themselves. At the same time we must keep one inescapable fact in mind: No country and no association of countries can guarantee international law and morality by means of a convention alone. As we well know, the last thirty years are strewn with the remains of burned-out and abandoned treaties and conventions. They were framed in a spirit of the highest idealism. By means of them the free nations
[Mr. Croll.l
sought to hold in check the black flood of barbarism which threatened, as it does today, to engulf the world.
The nations failed twice in our lifetime to restrain naked force by peaceful means. We learned, to our bitter loss, that a nation which signs a convention can also repudiate it. That is why we cannot let this genocide convention, or any international convention, lull us into a false sense of security. It is not an insurance policy against the future. And yet it can be a real weight to throw into the moral balance of the world. It carries the seeds of a new order for humanity. But those seeds may be barren, unless the free nations cultivate the ground for them.
I think the house has been told on another occasion that the free world has not been sleeping since 1945. Step by step we are building what may yet emerge as a new social order in the international sphere. Let me remind the house of UNRRA, the United Nations, the Marshall plan, ERP, NATO, the Colombo plan, and today the genocide convention. All these are steps along the road to international justice and morality.
I agree with those people who say we cannot impose democracy and liberty upon the beaten and backward nations of the world. We must first build them up to our level economically and socially. We must continue to strike at the causes of injustice, so that in time a convention like this should not be necessary.
In the light of past and present history it can be stated that this convention has been overdue for centuries. The genocide convention is now law-binding upon all nations that ratify the convention. It signifies humanity's determination once and for all to substitute the law of civilized society for that of the jungle.
I am happy to join with the house in endorsing this convention. We are thus giving leadership to those nations with whom we are usually associated in matters such as this. I pay tribute to the minister of external affairs for his efforts at the United Nations and his persistence and insistence that this government and this parliament ratify this convention.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION SIGNED BY CANADA ON NOVEMBER 28, 1949
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) has already indicated the heartfelt support which we accord to this motion for the adoption of the convention for the prevention of the crime of genocide. This is an occasion of really great importance in the history of mankind as we endeavour to move forward from what the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) referred

to as the law of the jungle to the light of full civilization. With the hon. member for Spadina we all hope the day will come when conventions like this may no longer be necessary, but we all recognize that by agreeing to a convention like this we are helping to sharpen the conscience of the world against what is referred to as the crime of genocide.
One of the reasons I felt I should like to say a few words at this time is that some of us feel that we must concern ourselves not only with the overt crime of genocide, against which we stand in all its forms; we should also take a stand at every possible opportunity against certain other practices which are inconsistent with a stand against the crime of genocide but which can be just as injurious and serious to the groups affected.
The definition of the crime of genocide in the convention we are now given the opportunity to endorse includes not only the overt destruction of racial and other groups as such, but any action injurious to a group or to a section of a group, or calculated to bring mental harm to any such group. I am reminded on this occasion of the words well known to all of us in the sermon on the mount. We remember how the Master suggested that the commandment of old, thou shalt not kill, did not mean in His view that people should only refrain from the overt act of murder; it meant that they should also refrain from hating their brothers or being angry with them in ways equally harmful. So I suggest that when things happen in other countries which we do not like, for example in South Africa today, and against which we might feel very strongly, we should feel equally strongly about any act of discrimination against any groups within our own country.
We need not go into the details of the form and type of discrimination that still takes place. I listened, as the house did, to the sad story given by the hon. member for Spadina and the many blots there have been on the story of mankind. The incidents he mentioned stand out and horrify us, whether they come from ancient times or from the days of the nazis. I hope this attempt to sharpen the conscience of the world, this attempt to sharpen our own conscience, will make us all feel equally sad at the realization that there are forms of discrimination against various groups, ethnic, racial, religious, social and economic, still being practised within our own country.
We who support and vote for this convention today, if we are to be consistent with our
Genocide Convention
vote, should take a stand at every opportunity against discrimination of any kind. If we are to see the day, if we are to have fulfilled that hope expressed by the previous speaker, when a convention like this may no longer be necessary, it is not only necessary that there be progress toward that ideal in other parts of the world; it is necessary that progress be made toward that same ideal in our own country.
I rose simply to express once again our wholehearted approval of this motion for the ratification of the convention to prevent the crime of genocide, and to express at the same time the hope that we will take all the steps we can in this country to do away with tire forms of discrimination that still exist against various minorities and groups within our land.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION SIGNED BY CANADA ON NOVEMBER 28, 1949
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, knowing the temperament of this parliament and of the Canadian people at large, I am not surprised to hear from every section of the house that there is unanimity of opinion in connection with the resolution submitted by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) for the ratification of the genocide convention. This resolution not only merits but calls for our every consideration because there are still clouds on the international horizon that threaten to create explosive situations which will produce horrible cases of mass killings which under the definition of the convention would be genocide.
Some countries unfortunately are still actively obsessed with a lust for power and domination. Other countries flagrantly ignore all human considerations and international regulations. Not only are they encouraging conditions which will produce genocide in the future, but they are actually committing the crime of genocide almost continuously. These conditions no doubt press upon the conscience of the free and peace-loving peoples of the world, the urgency to address themselves vigorously to safeguarding the common objectives, not only to prevent genocide but to help to make this world a better place in which to live.
The proposed legislation in my humble opinion is a definite step forward in that direction and will no doubt be unanimously approved by this parliament. We will then, Mr. Speaker, be able to take great pride in the fact that, in this, as well as in other similar international proposals, our country will be in the vanguard in setting an example for the rest of the world to follow.
It is perhaps necessary that in considering this legislation we should examine for a few moments the comparatively new expression not heretofore commonly known to the general

Genocide Convention
public, but which is now referred to as the crime of genocide, so we may better grasp the full significance and importance of ratifying this convention.
The term "genocide", originating as it does from two Latin words, means simply "the destruction of a group of people for no other reason than the fact that they belong to that particular group", which fact has already been so ably mentioned by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). The definition itself is found in article II of the convention. It reads:
In the present convention genocide means any of the following acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group as such:
(a)	killing members of the group;
(b)	causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group;
(c)	deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part;
(d)	imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group;
(e)	forcibly transferring children of the group to another group.
The diabolic reason for the slaughter may be a fanatical surge of racial, national or religious emotions; or it may be purely political; or it may be for reasons wholly unknown; or, as in most cases, it is committed without any reason whatsoever. The destruction may take the form of massacres, mass executions, starvation, restricting the birth rate, sterilization, segregation of the sexes, or the destruction of special characteristics of the group by various means.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the summarized and simple meaning of genocide; and the convention, by its own language in the preamble, "seeks to liberate mankind from this odious scourge."
As I had occasion to say during a previous debate in the house, the crime of genocide, although not known by that name, is not new in world history. Long before Carthage was destroyed by the Romans the crime of genocide had been committed. The Pharaohs of Egypt were wantonly guilty of the crime. The Roman destruction of religious groups in the lions' arena is a poignant and painful example of genocide. The Spanish inquisition, the massacre of St. Bartholomew's day, are examples of a crime which long should have been outlawed.
This horrible crime was committed not only in ancient days, or during the middle ages, as has been so fully described, but what is very sad is the fact that the crime has been frequently committed during our own lifetime. Many of our contemporaries witnessed the wanton massacres of the Armenians by the Ottoman empire on several occasions and the massacre of Christian Assyrians in Iraq, as
[Mr. Crestohl.l
well as the long list of victims already mentioned. More recently, we have witnessed the Ethiopian massacres by Mussolini, the Chinese massacres by Japan and the Jewish massacres by the nazis. Acts such as these throughout the centuries have left black pages in our history books. We search the records in vain for some action by world leadership to prevent the commission of acts of genocide or to punish the guilty.
It is of record, though, that not only in the past, but even quite recently, civilized peoples did not altogether condone the brutalities of those guilty of genocide. They never failed piously to utter protests, hold some meetings, offer some prayers, and a few foreign governments even showed some courage by sending diplomatic notes. Nothing more direct or more vigorous was ever done.
Under the guise of its being a matter of domestic jurisdiction, these crimes were repeatedly committed while civilization stood aghast and shouted "shame", but unfortunately did nothing more.
Human beings are normally disturbed by a calamity in which one or more persons are killed. The degree of shock and distress is increasingly accentuated by the number of fellow human beings who are accidentally killed. Imagine, therefore, Mr. Speaker, the frightful shudder that goes through a person when he hears of wanton mass murder involving over ten million innocent victims. It is no secret, and it has already been mentioned several times today in the house, that modern civilization cringes in shame when we hear of crematoria, mass graves, gas chambers and other such hideous implements of murder.
The studied, scientific and systematic brutalities of the nazis shocked the conscience of the twentieth century. It required an upheaval such as this, almost a volcanic violation of human sensibilities, to shake and shame the decent world into seeking means more vigorous than gasps, vocal protests and pious diplomatic notes, to prevent the commission of such crimes in the future. Is it, therefore, not a natural consequence that modern civilization should press for the creation of international machinery to prevent a repetition of these acts? The genocide convention is for the time being a partial answer to this anguished demand.
It is in my humble opinion not merely the product of international statesmen or the wisdom of their cool and calculated thinking. It is rather an outcry from the grass root level of human beings whose emotions have been violated and are not tempered by delicate, legal, diplomatic or international niceties.

The call for a genocide convention is urgently being pressed for and supported by the most important religious, labour, veteran and civic groups in the leading countries of the world. In the United States, for example, the convention is being pleaded for and supported by every humanitarian organization in the country. I have before me a list of over sixty of these international organizations, the most recognized and most important in the country. To indicate the types of these organizations I should like to mention only a few. They are: the national conference of Christians and Jews, the Catholic association for international peace, the federated council of churches of Christ in America, the American Federation of Labour, the congress of industrial organizations, the American Legion, the world Jewish congress, the American veterans' committee, the general federation of women's clubs, the young women's Christian associations of America, the Catholic association for international peace and countless others.
In our own country, and in other countries, similar groups have likewise urged the adoption and the ratification of the genocide convention. It is today a universal outcry, and at long last it is being seriously dealt with.
The theory of non-intervention in a matter of so-called domestic jurisdiction, Mr. Speaker, to which I referred a few moments ago, is no longer tenable with respect to crimes which are universally acknowledged as inhuman and immoral, and this notwithstanding the fact that traditionally criminal law has been considered as an expression of the right of a state to define and punish acts, which in its judgment are contrary to public order within its borders. International law of modern times has recognized certain crimes which it declared to be international, and regards them as directed against public order not of any one given country, but as against public order of the entire family of nations. The crime of piracy, for example, the crime of international slave trade, the illegal production of and trade in narcotics, white slavery and similar crimes belong to that category. These are the subject matter of various charters, conventions, treaties and pacts under the United Nations Organization, and are governed by international law.
Within the past number of years we have been forcibly reminded by the Nuremberg judgments that to this category of international crimes also belong war crimes and crimes against humanity. Consequently, Mr. Speaker, with the advance of civilization, the crime of genocide should be similarly classi-
Genocide Convention
fled and outlawed. Our country should, of course, be amongst the first to support this view.
Someone once very appropriately said that important lessons are frequently learned from great sacrifices. Martyrdom in history is perhaps the most formidable example we have to prove that the sacrifices of these saintly men and women helped pave the road for the creation and preservation of those principles that civilization holds dear today. Men and women were burned at the stake, tortured to death, and gave up their lives rather than swerve from their beliefs and their convictions. We have indeed learned great lessons from them.
I should like to refer for a few moments to sacrifices made to a degree heretofore unheard of in the annals of history, and which were not made in the dim past but during the past two decades, in our own lifetime. Let us see, Mr. Speaker, what lessons, if any, we have learned from these sacrifices, whether millions will have died in vain without contemporary history having reaped any lessons from these sacrifices.
Before and after 1939 the democratic countries witnessed the commission of the crime of genocide both in Ethiopia by Mussolini and in Germany by Hitler. Civilization stood idly by. Perhaps it gasped in sympathy; nevertheless I repeat it stood idly by. This should never occur again. If, for example, the nations of the world had seriously warned Mussolini or Hitler that what they were doing would be internationally challenged, and their countries would be isolated from the rest of the world by the imposition of international sanctions, we might not only have prevented the most flagrant case of genocide in history but we might have been able to avert world war II. What the world suffered for not doing so could almost, in the judgment of devout believers, be a lesson in retribution.
If, for example, sanctions had been threatened and effectively imposed between 1934 and 1939, the world would have known where dictatorships were going. In my judgment it is doubtful whether, with the complete isolation of these bandits early enough in their careers of crime, they would have been able to secure the materials and supplies to create their weapons for conquest, which they were otherwise able to build up between 1934 and 1939.
It is therefore my respectful submission, Mr. Speaker, that the convention should go further than it does. By its present terms it threatens trial and punishment of the guilty, but refers rather weakly in article VII to the possibility of arresting the commission of the crimes once they are commenced. By

Genocide Convention
the time the perpetrators can be brought to trial, it may be too late. Some vigorous provisions should be included which would prevent the commission of the crimes or stop them once they are started.
The security council of the United Nations, which is continually in session, should most cautiously scrutinize every act or manoeuvre which might lead to the suspicion that genocide is being committed or is about to be committed. They should be given adequate power and authority to call for an immediate cessation of those acts which may lead to, or in fact may be, genocide. Moreover the council should be given express authority, without the necessity of waiting for a meeting of the plenary session of the general assembly, to threaten effective international sanctions if their directives and orders are disobeyed. This would be a direct attempt to prevent acts of genocide, and to arrest them if started.
I respectfully urge our representatives to the United Nations to deal with this matter just as soon as the appropriate opportunity presents itself. Such action would be consistent with our country's views in matters of this kind and would, I am certain, be hailed by all the freedom-loving peoples of the world.
The United Nations has, for example, an opportunity today to prevent the crime of genocide which is being committed in several countries. During the past twenty-four months Iraq has been, and is now, in the process of committing acts which are genocide under the interpretation of the convention. Dangerous indications appear in a number of other countries, and unless the United Nations Organization takes the situation firmly in hand, acts of mass murder by violence or by means set forth in the definition of genocide may be committed in the countries of North Africa, Egypt, Iran, Aden, South Africa, Greece, North and South Korea, in Yugoslavia and the Baltic states.
A short time ago Greek reds kidnapped 28,000 Greek children and took them behind the iron curtain, solely because of their nationality. Chinese reds and North Koreans have slaughtered whole groups of clergymen and children because of their religion. In the Baltic states more than a million persons have been killed or exiled because of their national origin. These acts, Mr. Speaker, are preambles to genocide, if they are not indeed genocide according to the convention. Such horrors need little enhancement to ripen into the planned destruction of an entire group.
Preventive provisions in the convention, in my opinion, are therefore even more important than punitive provisions. I am hopeful that this phase will be given active consideration by international statesmen.

Some preventive steps may be found in articles III and IV of the convention. Article III sets forth that the following acts should be punishable: (a) genocide; (b) conspiracy to commit genocide; (c) direct and public incitement to commit genocide; (d) attempt to commit genocide; (e) complicity in genocide. Article IV sets forth that persons committing genocide or any of the other acts enumerated in article III should be punishable, whether they are constitutionally responsible rulers, public officials or private individuals. This is perhaps the first time in the history of international affairs, Mr. Speaker, that a warning is proclaimed that constitutionally responsible rulers are no longer immune, even in their own domains, from the responsibility for committing crimes. In other words the myth in international law that "the king can do no wrong" has been substantially modified.
No responsible head of a state will be able to commit with impunity acts which are being labelled by this convention as crimes against civilization.
I should like to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that the machinery for implementing the convention as set out in article VI appears to be, in my judgment, a little vague. I now read from the convention itself:
Persons charged with genocide or any of the other acts enumerated in article III shall be tried by a competent tribunal of the state in the territory where the act was committed, or by such international penal tribunal as may have jurisdiction with respect to those contracting parties which shall have accepted its jurisdiction.
It is, of course, not difficult to conceive that a criminal court of any particular state might have a problem in trying its ruler, leader, statesmen or anyone else. Domestic courts can unfortunately be tampered with or neutralized by legislation, as we see in the case of South Africa today.
A procedure much more definite and much more independent is therefore required if clause VI is to have any effective meaning. Consequently I direct attention in clause VI to the following words: "such international penal tribunal as may have jurisdiction" and so forth. This wording implies the use of an international penal tribunal.
I understand that the creation of an international criminal court has recently been recommended. I hope it will be established. The committee on international law appointed by the Canadian Bar Association has given the matter much study. This is one of the most important committees of the Canadian Bar Association, since it is composed of past presidents of the association and is presided over by Chief Justice McRuer of Ontario.
It is my hope, Mr. Speaker, that this committee will not only recommend amendments

to our own Criminal Code to enable our courts to deal with those charged with the crime of genocide, but will also support the establishment of an international criminal court and recommend a procedure making it possible to bring before it, try and punish offenders, irrespective of their station and importance in their own country. The establishment of such a court might really put some teeth into the convention and would make of it something more than an instrument of mere wishful thinking, noble as that in itself might be.
The genocide convention, Mr. Speaker, was originally brought to the attention of the United States as early as 1946, shortly after the United Nations Organization was first convened. The convention was adopted unanimously on December 9, 1948. Its coming into force, however, was suspended until at least 20 member nations, by acts of their respective parliaments, would ratify the convention. Those ratifications were, unfortunately, rather slow in coming in. Finally on January 12, 1951, it being the ninetieth day after the twentieth instrument of ratification was deposited with the Secretary General of the United Nations in accordance with the terms of the convention, the convention was finally ratified.
Since then many more countries have ratified the convention and I believe there are at the present time some 36 nations which have approved it. Our own country was among the first to sign the original instrument, and our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) is now submitting this resolution for Canada likewise to deposit with the Secretary General of the United Nations the requisite document indicating that the people and the parliament of Canada have ratified the convention which it signed on November 28, 1949. This step is consistent, as I said at the commencement of my remarks, with the high moral level of our country and the reputation which it enjoys in the eyes of the civilized peoples of the world.
This example, I hope, will now be followed by the rest of the members of the United Nations who have not yet ratified, so that the entire civilized world will not only declare its abhorrence of the crime of genocide, and condemn it, but will also declare itself ready to punish all individuals, groups and even nations who will resort to the unspeakable crime of mass murder.
I have one more point that I should like to add, Mr. Speaker, and it is this. Since our country has acquired a position of preeminence for its humanitarian views and as a fearless champion of justice, it is all the more important for our parliament to
Genocide Convention
ratify the convention, because those countries which have not yet approved it may look to us for guidance and leadership. Our hesitation to sign, or suspension of this action, will cause much eyebrow raising amongst those countries, who will wonder why Canada has not yet signed.
There have been some questions raised as to why the United States, Great Britain and other democracies have not yet adopted the necessary legislation to approve the genocide pact. There appears to be no explanation other than casual indifference, or a belief, to some extent, that the pact is not necessary, or that it may be inoperative. No reason whatsoever can justify a refusal to declare the crime of genocide repulsive to civilization. What are these delinquent countries waiting for? Have their sensibilities not yet been sufficiently violated? Or has the passing of only a few years already dimmed their revulsion at what has occurred? Surely those democracies who cling so jealously to their ideals should be the very first to vigorously urge universal condemnation of the crime of genocide. Hesitation obviously has the effect of giving encouragement to those countries which practise genocide in our own days.
I am therefore hopeful, Mr. Speaker, and sincerely pray that with the adoption of this legislation by our parliament, the necessary stimulus will be given to the rest of the democracies who have not yet approved this convention and that, in the not too distant future, twentieth century civilization will be able to record the universal condemnation of a crime that has plagued human history, and the fact that henceforth the crime of genocide will be effectively outlawed and never again practised by man.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION SIGNED BY CANADA ON NOVEMBER 28, 1949
speechtext:
-I think I should say a few words on this important resolution and express the view of the government with respect to it. Before doing so, however, I should like to deny the soft impeachment of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) that

Genocide Convention
my absence from the house over the last day or two has had anything to do with what he called political genocide. Genocide, Mr. Speaker, is mass destruction or the intention to commit mass destruction. My purposes, during my absence for the last few days, have been entirely constructive.
The resolution to approve the Canadian ratification of the convention on the prevention and punishment of the crime of genocide, as the previous speakers have pointed out, has already been considered in detail by the standing committee on external affairs and has been reported to the house without amendment. The genocide convention which is before us was the first convention to be prepared by the United Nations and opened for signature by states throughout the world. The text was unanimously adopted by the general assembly of the United Nations on December 9, 1948. Canada's representatives at the first part of the third session of the general assembly in Paris in 1948 were among those who supported the principle that the genocide convention should receive the widest possible application. Canada signed the convention on November 28, 1949, and it came into effect on January 12,	1951, 90 days
after the deposit of twenty instruments of ratification or accession without reservation. As has been pointed out, a total of 36 states have now ratified or acceded, thirty without reservation and six, unfortunately, with reservations. The states which annexed reservations are: Bulgaria, Roumania, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary and the Philippines. The genocide convention is important not only because of the nature of the matter with which it deals but because it is the first international convention, prepared at any time, which seeks to define an international criminal offence. This means essentially an offence to be prevented and punished by all the states which adhere to the convention and for which they may be held to account by other states.
The crime is defined in article II, which has already been read to the house. It reads:
Acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such...
As it has already been done very eloquently, Mr. Speaker, I do not need to recall to the house some of the horrible examples of genocide we have had in the past, especially the recent abominable instance of the practices of the nazis during the 1930's and during the war. Their systematic and ruthless policy, designed to uproot and exterminate a whole people, the Jewish people, makes one of the most tragic chapters in the whole of human history. A glorious footnote, however, has

been written to that chapter, in the emergence and the establishment of the state of Israel.
There have been other examples. Perhaps I might read at this point a communication which indicates that genocide is not yet eradicated from the world, especially from that part of the world behind the iron curtain. This communication for obvious reasons, which will commend themselves to the house, will have to remain anonymous. It is addressed to me, and reads as follows:
My wife and I recently spent a week end in X-
X being a city in Russia.
-where we were shepherded around. An incident occurred as our train was leaving the city which I thought worthy of recording.
Our train was forced to stop a moment as we were pulling out of the station. I looked from my window and saw, six or seven tracks away, a line of cattle cars, but they were not filled with cattle; they were filled with women. There was an aperture of about a foot and a half between the sides and the roof, and from this opening peered hopelessly out the emaciated faces, framed by clawing hands, of numbers of women. There w'ere soldiers at the track side with fixed bayonets so there could be no mistaking the meaning.
It was just a moment's pause. Then our train moved on, but it was as if the corner of a curtain had been lifted, permitting a brief glance into the cesspool. Where these poor unfortunates came from, or where they were going, we can only guess -perhaps from Estonia; destination, just the east.
It is that kind of thing, Mr. Speaker, that this convention, inadequate though it may be in many respects, is designed to prevent or at least to make more difficult. The human race has, we must hope, become more civilized, and the inherent rights of the individual and of minority groups have become more important; they have become protected under domestic law, particularly under the laws of democratic states. We must hope that in the future that protection under domestic law may be reinforced by international convention and international law. This convention is designed to do just that. Up to the present these rights have not been protected as a matter of international law, and I hope this convention will at least be helpful in that essential process.
The contracting states under the convention undertake to prosecute persons guilty of genocide in their own countries or, in the alternative, to surrender them to an international penal tribunal if and when such a tribunal is established. This latter obligation does not arise at once in any case or by virtue of the ratification of this treaty, since the contracting parties would also have to agree by a separate convention to accept the jurisdiction of such an international tribunal. For practical purposes, then, and particularly

because the establishment of such an international penal tribunal is problematical at this time, it may be said that the scheme of the convention is that contracting states accept genocide as an international crime and undertake to punish offenders in their own courts.
As has been pointed out, however, the convention contains one provision in article IX, which has some teeth in it, in the sense that it affords a means by which one contracting state can bring another contracting state before the international court of justice. The international court of justice-which has no jurisdiction over individuals as distinct from states, and which also has no criminal jurisdiction of any kind-would have no power to pronounce on the guilt or innocence of any person, but under this article it might give a declaratory judgment as to whether the respondent state was, in fact, carrying out its obligations generally under the convention.
The communist countries have consistently refused to accept the compulsory jurisdiction of the international court of justice, and in line with this general position these countries -and also the Philippine republic-have made reservations refusing to be bound by this article.
A few countries objected to those reservations, and the objections which were made have been responsible for hesitation and some delay on the part of certain states to ratify this treaty. To clear up these difficulties the Secretary General of the United Nations asked the general assembly for a directive at its fifth session in 1950 in regard to the significance of reservations of this kind.	The assembly then, as many hon.
members know, decided to refer the question to the international court of justice, and it was hoped that the court would give an opinion which would clarify the whole situation. This hope was not, I confess, entirely realized in the event. The court by a majority decision merely stated that any state could be regarded as a party to the convention while maintaining a reservation, notwithstanding the objection of other states, if the reservation could be considered as "compatible with the objects and purposes of the convention." The court refused to state whether or not the reservations in question were "compatible," and said that this depended upon a subjective appraisal of the effect of the reservation by each state.
Therefore the decision in one sense did not carry us much farther forward. The present position then is that if Canada were now to object to the communist reservations
55704-154J
Genocide Convention
on the ground that they were in fact "incompatible" the communist countries, as well as some other countries, might maintain that they were "compatible." In these circumstances-and we gave a great deal of consideration to this difficulty-it appeared desirable to the government that Canada should now ratify the convention without reference to the reservations even though this might involve our acceptance of them by legal implication.
The language of the reservation is such that no country which has made the reservation under article IX can hale a non-reserving country on a charge under the convention before the international court of justice without the non-reserving country's consent. That is a very important consideration. The reservations made under article IX are identical, and I shall read the terms used by Bulgaria: Bulgaria does not consider as binding upon itself the provisions of article IX . . . and declares that, as regards the international court's jurisdiction . . ! Bulgaria will . . . maintain the position that in each particular case the agreement of all parties to the dispute is essential, for the submission of any particular dispute to the international court for decision.
In other words it seems to me to be clear from the wording of that reservation that Canada, for instance, could not be brought before the international court of justice on a charge of violation of the convention we are now considering, by a country like Bulgaria, which has made this reservation, without the consent of Canada itself.
The genocide convention is possibly the most important source of new international criminal law which has developed since the last war. Other sources of this law are the Nuremberg principles based upon the charter and judgments of the Nuremberg tribunal, which were formulated by the international law commission of the United Nations, and also the proposed code of offences against the peace and security of mankind, which is still under consideration in the United Nations.
Since it is desirable, I think, that there should be world-wide acceptance that genocide is a crime, and since the force of the convention as a source of international law depends upon its general acceptance by states, the conclusion may be logically drawn that it is best to have the widest possible acceptance by states of this convention as a source of law, even although there may be a refusal by some states to accept the enforcement provision in article IX.
The following question has arisen, causing some anxiety I believe in the committee, and it has been referred to today by the hon.

Genocide Convention
member for Peel (Mr. Graydon). The question is this: Is any legislation required in Canada to implement within our own borders the obligations which our country will undertake under the convention? On this important matter I should like to quote the opinion of the deputy minister of justice, to whom this was referred for an opinion. He wrote as follows:
You have asked for my opinion as to the nature of the legislation, if any, that may be required to implement the convention on the prevention and punishment of the crime of genocide to which Canada will, I understand1, shortly become a signatory-
This letter, by the way, was written before we actually signed the convention, and not in connection with its consideration for ratification.
You also asked for a confirmation of your assumption that no legislation on the part of the provinces would be required to implement the convention.
Dealing with your last query first, in my view, the provinces are not required to introduce legislation to implement the provisions of a convention which relates in its entirety to criminal law.
I am further of the opinion that no legislation is required by Canada, at this time, to implement this convention. In this connection, I would direct your attention to the wording of article V of the convention. I do not think any legislation is "necessary," inasmuch as I cannot conceive of any act of commission or omission occurring in Canada as falling within the definition of the crime of genocide contained in article II of the convention, that would not be covered by the relevant section in the Criminal Code.
It was only after we received this opinion back in 1949 that we signed this convention which is now before the House of Commons for approval.
There is another point which has been of equal concern to members of the standing committee on external affairs, and which also was mentioned by the hon. member for Peel. I refer to the meaning of the words "mental harm" in subparagraph (b) of article II of the convention. This article defines the offence as I have already quoted it, and I shall repeat the definition for convenience:
Acts committed with Intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such. . .
These are the governing words of the definition, and consequently they control and limit the effect of the specific list of acts which follow those governing words. The second of these listed acts reads:
(b) Causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group.
It is the words "mental harm" which have caused some uneasiness in some minds. My understanding, Mr. Speaker, is that the words "mental harm" cannot mean anything but physical injury to the mental faculties.

The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), who has taken a keen interest in this convention, pointed out before the standing committee on external affairs that these two words were originally introduced into the definition at the request of the Chinese delegate to the United Nations who was concerned with the practice of the Japanese of administering opium to the Chinese people as a means of weakening their resistance in the Sino-Japanese war.
Of course the administering of opium to a racial group which would involve physical injury to the mental faculties would come within the definition I have just quoted. I cannot myself conceive that mental harm can be caused to persons with intent to destroy in whole or in part a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, without physical injury to the mental faculties of such persons.
I therefore suggest to the house that the use of the words "mental harm" would and should be interpreted, as a measure of both our domestic and our international responsibility, as meaning "physical injury to the mental faculties".
My attention has also been directed to another point which I think might be cleared up at this time. I refer to a decision handed down by the United States supreme court concerning the constitutional validity of a law of the state of Illinois. It concerned a statute of that state and it was not a decision on the interpretation of the genocide convention. However, the judgment did comment on the genocide convention and might have given the impression that while genocide is of course, literally, the murder of a race, by extension it could be applied to any act detrimental to the welfare of any identifiable group, whether the lines of identification are religious, racial, cultural or national, and that it might apply to crimes against such groups short of extermination and might therefore really be aimed against any concerted determined discrimination against a minority.
While I do not think any of us would condone discrimination of this kind in any way, shape or form, I think that interpretation of this convention is going too far; that is, that it could be interpreted as applying to discrimination against a minority.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION SIGNED BY CANADA ON NOVEMBER 28, 1949
speechtext: Some Canadians have taken that interpretation.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION SIGNED BY CANADA ON NOVEMBER 28, 1949
speechtext:
That is not the interpretation we would give it. And while I would not have anything I say on this point interpreted as approving or condoning discrimination of this kind in any shape or form, we would

have our own way, I hope, of dealing with such discrimination. I think it would be undesirable to leave the impression that it could be brought under this convention, or that this convention could be used properly for this particular purpose.
In conclusion may I say that the possibility of the crime of genocide being committed in Canada seems to me to be extremely remote. I stress the fact that the broad purpose of this convention is to bring the law throughout the world up to the standard which I think we may say without boasting happily exists already in our own country. In approving this convention unanimously, which I hope parliament will do, we will be proclaiming throughout the world that genocide is considered by us to be a monstrous crime. We will be doing something to make it more difficult for any other country to commit that crime.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: DISCIPLINE AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
When this section was under discussion during the resolution stage I directed attention to an injustice which has existed for many years in relation to junior warrant or petty officers or junior commissioned officers. I suggested that that injustice should be removed by the removal of the limitations placed upon the earnings of retired officers who find employment in the civil service. I had hoped that consideration would be given to my suggestion.
As the amendment now stands it would be possible for two or three men to retire on the same day with the same length of service and take exactly the same positions in the civil service. If one of those men was a senior officer, a brigadier or admiral, his pension would be greater than that drawn by an officer of the junior rank. If the brigadier took a position in the civil service he would be entitled to draw pay from the civil service along with his pension to the extent that the combined pay and pension did not exceed the pay of the rank which he had held at today's rates of pay and allowances.
The same thing would apply to the captain or warrant officer, but if this man took a similar position with the civil service you would have a ridiculous situation created. The senior officer would be able to draw his entire pay from the civil service as well as his entire pension because the combined

Canadian Forces Act
amounts would not reach the level of the pay and allowances for his rank, but the warrant officer or captain taking a similar position would find that he was entitled to a much smaller amount because the pay of a captain or warrant officer would be considerably less. He would draw his pay from the civil service but his pension would be reduced because the combined civil service pay and pension would exceed the pay of that particular rank at the present time.
This irregularity and injustice has existed for many years, and I had hoped that the minister would be prepared to remove it when bringing in his amendments. I hope consideration will still be given to doing this. I hope the parliamentary assistant will be able to say that the limitations have either been removed altogether or that there will be a fixed limitation which will be equitable to all ranks of retired persons. I hope the parliamentary assistant will be able to make that announcement today as well as the very satisfactory announcement he has just made concerning the other clauses. Then I would have no further objections.
